transcript: I think Slam Frank might have been funnier when it didn't exist. For those just joining us, this is a musical comedy about Anne Frank in the style of Hamilton, but it's essentially a satire of performative wokeness reimagining Anne Frank as Latina. It began as a series of rage baiting TikToks from the writer, Andrew Fox, and he arguably committed to the bit too close to the sun. So to be honest, I didn't really like this show, but considering the slam Frank TikTok account sometimes likes to mock me in the comment section of my own videos, it's possible that I'm not totally exempt from the satire in the show. So I had to consider if that was contributing to my reaction at all, but I don't think it did. I'm sure it's not a coincidence that the slam Frank TikTok series came on the heels of the 2024 election, when a lot of people on the left were taking a beat to reflect on whether the infighting and the chasing moral purity was actually creating the meaningful change that we hoped it would. And because of that reflection, I'd like to think that I wasn't biased against this musical because it was critiquing the left. In fact, I think I was fairly receptive to it. And positive or negative, I definitely found that original TikTok series to be a pretty fascinating case study in our political moment, and that idea is still somewhere at the core of this Off-Broadway musical. But on multiple levels, I think it goes awry. I would be lying if I said the show didn't get some laughs out of me here and there. It definitely did. But even after its developmental run last year, this final product still feels like it's throwing everything at the wall to see what sticks. And with an almost two hour run time, it starts to feel like it's making the same point over and over in a way that I found, frankly, kind of exhausting. The musical uses a framing device where it's a show within a show. So everything we see is through the lens of this fictional artistic director, who's super sanctimonious-woke, and out of touch. So on paper, the idea is that they're not mocking marginalized people, they're mocking people like this artistic director. And there are many times when that works really well. But it can also be treacherous. Using that sort of blanket deniability as a shield can cause writers and directors to lose track of it a little bit, slip up, and present certain moments in a way that blurs the line between punching up and punching down. But even if we dismiss that and say, “yeah, it's pushing buttons on purpose,” “that's the point. Don't be so sensitive.” Even then, I would still argue that muddling the intention of who's mocking who and to what end is a storytelling issue. It blunts the satire and weakens the Comedy. Credit where it's due, this seems to be one of the only major productions to play in New York theatre recently to take a meaningful stance against lsrael. But even that element of the show feels very jumbled and undercooked in its execution. Again, don't get me wrong, there are a lot of strong and funny moments throughout the show, but a big part of why I think it feels so messy and bloated is that this concept was never built to sustain a full length show. In fact, arguably, it was never built to sustain a show of any length. It seems to me that the real performance isn't happening off Broadway at the Orpheum Theatre. It happened already online for all of us to see. And sort of like how a meme stops being funny and cool when it starts to go mainstream, it seems to me that this was a piece of online performance art that essentially ended the moment that tickets for the “actual performance” went on sale. And this off Broadway show is kind of just the echo of it.
